text:
By 1849 the use of Alviso as the main freight depot for the southern Bay Area had been realized. In this year the town site was surveyed by C. S. Lyman for Jacob D. Hoppe, Charles B. Marvin, Kimball H. Dimmick and Robert S. Neligh who had acquired a tract of land for this purpose. Lots were put up for sale at $600 each, a large commercial center was planned, and for a time there was even talk of a canal being constructed to San Jose (Gudde 1969, Munro-Fraser 1881). Little interest was shown for any of these ventures, however, and it was soon evident that the plans of these mem had come to naught.
In December of 1849 a steam powered vessel first came into use on the Guadalupe River. A scow named the "Sacramento" was fitted with an engine and machinery and the boat was soon plying a route between San Francisco and Alviso. The trip took ten hours one-way with the cost of passenger fare being forty dollars. For an additional ten dollars one could travel by stage to San Jose (Munro-Fraser 1881). By the spring of 1850, numerous steamboats were traveling in and out of Alviso. This, combined with an influx of settlers created by the gold rush, gave a boost to Alviso. Soon, wharves and at least six warehouses had been or were in the process of being constructed at the port and in 1851 Richard Carr opened the town's first store. There quickly followed the American Hotel, the Four Musketeers Hotel, another store, a black-smith shop, and a number of residences (Munro-Fraser 1881).
An act to incorporate the town of Alviso was approved on March 26, 1852. A board of trustees was established as were the offices of treasurer and marshall. Property taxes soon came to bear on the inhabitants of the town at the rate of 25¢ per hundred dollars of assessed value (Munro-Fraser 1881).
The town continued to prosper as a shipping center until the mid 1860's. In 1864 the San Francisco-San Jose Railroad was completed and travel diverted from Alviso. Foote (1888:296) states that the town almost became deserted. The Southern Pacific Railroad revived business somewhat in 1876 when it began service through the town, but Alviso was not destined to become the great metropolis once envisioned by its founders. In 1881 J.P. Munro-Fraser wrote:
"There are some residents who are still sanguine, and predict a great future for the little town. We, unhappily, are under the impression that the true legend is Ichabod! Ichabod! The glory is departed!" (Munro-Fraser: 251).
